name: Shankari Devi Temple, Trincomalee
deity: The Goddess as Shankari Devi (Indrakshi), the Shakti Peetha of Lanka
period: Named first among the eighteen Maha Shakti Peethas in the stotram ascribed to Adi Shankara (8th century); the historic shrine was destroyed in the 17th century and the Goddess is honoured again at Koneswaram since the 20th
dynasty: Ancient tradition; Tamil Hindu patronage of the Koneswaram precinct; modern reconstruction
summary: First of the eighteen Maha Shakti Peethas, Shankari Devi is the Goddess of Lanka, honoured on Swami Rock beside the Koneswaram temple, where a seat broken by the Portuguese is worshipped again above the Trincomalee sea.

sections.history: Shankari Devi is named first in the Ashtadasha Shakti Peetha Stotram, the hymn ascribed to Adi Shankara that lists eighteen great seats of the Goddess and opens with the words Lankayam Shankari Devi, meaning in Lanka, Shankari Devi. Tradition places her seat on Swami Rock at Trincomalee, on the same headland as the Koneswaram temple of Shiva, and pilgrims have long visited the two together as Shakti and Shiva. The historic shrine did not survive the colonial age. Portuguese forces under Constantino de Sá de Noronha pulled down the temples of the rock in the early seventeenth century, with sources giving 1622 or 1624, and the stone went into Fort Frederick. Worship was revived in the twentieth century, and the Goddess is honoured today in a rebuilt shrine beside Koneswaram.
sections.architecture: Swami Rock is a headland that ends in a sheer cliff, falling some 120 metres to the sea, and the shrine of the Goddess stands within the same sacred precinct as Koneswaram, reached through the gates of Fort Frederick. What worshippers see today is a modern reconstruction in the Dravidian manner of the island's Tamil Hindu temples, with a sanctum for the Goddess and a gateway and sculpted ornament in the familiar southern style. Little of the original medieval stonework is known to remain in place. What endures is the setting itself: the rock, the salt wind and the long view over Trincomalee's great natural harbour.
sections.legends: In the Puranic story Sati, daughter of Daksha, gives up her life at her father's sacrifice after he insults Shiva. Shiva wanders the world carrying her body in his grief, and Vishnu's discus divides it so that its parts fall in sacred places, each afterwards worshipped as a Shakti Peetha. Lists commonly say that at Trincomalee it was the groin of Sati that fell, while a verse of the Pitha Nirnaya names the anklet for the seat in Lanka, giving the Goddess there as Indrakshi and the Bhairava as Rakshaseshwara. This is why the same seat is remembered as both Shankari and Indrakshi, and why other places in Sri Lanka, such as Nainativu in the north, also appear in the tradition. Local belief further links Swami Rock with Ravana, the devout king of Lanka who worshipped Shiva.
sections.festivals: Navaratri, the nine nights of the Goddess in autumn and closing with Vijayadashami, is the natural season of devotion to Shankari Devi, and Fridays are dear to her devotees. As part of the Koneswaram precinct the shrine also shares in Maha Shivaratri and in the festivals of the Tamil calendar kept on the rock. Specific observances at the Goddess's own shrine are not firmly documented, and dates follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm locally.
sections.experience: The visit is as much a climb to a headland as to a shrine. Pass through the fort gates, walk out along Swami Rock with the sea falling away on either side, and come to the Goddess after greeting Shiva at Koneswaram, as pilgrims have long done. Many devotees recite the opening line of the stotram, Lankayam Shankari Devi, at her threshold. Knowing how much was lost here gives the quiet shrine a particular tenderness, and the open sky and sea make it easy to understand why this was chosen as the first seat of the Goddess.

visit.timings: Fort Frederick, through which the rock is reached, is reported open from early morning to late evening, and the shrines keep the usual morning and evening worship with a midday pause. Confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected, with shoulders and knees covered. Men may be asked to remove shirts before entering the shrine, and footwear is left outside. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum. The approach passes through an army-managed fort, so follow posted signs, and ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The shrine is on Swami Rock inside Fort Frederick in Trincomalee town, less than 3 km from Trincomalee railway station, which has services from Colombo. Colombo lies roughly 260 km away by road, and Bandaranaike International Airport near Colombo is the main international gateway. Foreign visitors are usually asked to buy a ticket at the counter by the car park before the fort.
